analysis.one_liner: Cuts sulfur and nitrogen pollution from power plants, factories, cars, and diesel fuel to stop acid rain.
analysis.headline: The acid rain bill drew 158 cosponsors from both parties but never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and its goal became law a year later in the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced every state to cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions from coal-fired power plants in two steps, with federal limits imposed automatically if a state failed. It also capped sulfur in diesel fuel, tightened tailpipe standards for cars and trucks, and created a fund — paid for by a small fee on fossil-fuel generation — to shield residential customers from the resulting rate increases. Six subcommittees held hearings, but the full committee never voted, and the bill died there; Congress passed an acid rain program the next year through a different bill.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal-fired power plants — especially in the Northeast, where acid rain was damaging lakes, forests, and buildings — would get cleaner air as utilities cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide. Residents would also gain from lower sulfur diesel and cleaner tailpipes. The bill specifically protected residential electric customers: a federal fund would cover rate increases above 10%, low-income customers got extra protection from the fee, and states had to spread rate increases evenly. Communities dependent on coal jobs got grants for cleanup technology designed partly to avoid fuel switching.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwind residents, ratepayers, and coal communities

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state to cut sulfur dioxide emissions from coal-fired power plants to 2.0 pounds per million Btu by 1994 and 1.2 by 1998, with nitrogen oxide limits of 0.6 by 1998 — and if a state fails to file or get an approved plan, the EPA imposes those exact limits automatically.

Extends the cleanup beyond utilities: industrial boilers, major industrial process sources, new coal-burning plants, and, on the roads, tighter nitrogen oxide standards for cars and trucks, hydrocarbon standards for trucks, onboard vapor-recovery controls, and a cap of 0.05 percent sulfur in motor vehicle diesel fuel after January 1, 1991.

Protects residential electric customers from the cost of cleanup: a federal subsidy program pays the share of rate increases attributable to sulfur dioxide compliance that exceeds 10%, states must spread increases evenly across residential customers and levelize them over time, and the fee that funds the program must include provisions to protect low-income customers and exempts hydro and nuclear generation.

Creates an Acid Deposition Control Fund and authorizes EPA grants to help plant owners adopt innovative pollution-control technology, with eligibility criteria that weigh employment dislocation from fuel switching — a direct nod to coal-dependent regions.

analysis.who_pays: Coal-burning electric utilities would bear the direct cost of emission controls, and their industrial and commercial customers would feel rate increases that the residential subsidy program does not cover. High-sulfur coal producers would lose demand as plants cleaned up or switched fuel. Refineries would pay to desulfurize diesel, and automakers would install new emission-control equipment. Residential customers would pay the small generation fee (up to half a mill per kilowatt hour) and any rate increase beyond the 10% the subsidy covers, though only through the end of 1997.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal-burning utilities, high-sulfur coal producers, refineries, automakers

drawbacks.text: The cost does not disappear — it moves. A fee of up to half a mill per kilowatt hour on fossil-fuel generation funds the residential subsidies, which sunset after 1997, and any residential rate increase above the 10% threshold, plus all increases for business and industrial customers, would land on electricity bills.

The subsidy design blunts the incentive to clean up cheaply: utilities whose compliance costs pass EPA review get ratepayer money to cover them, which shields the industry from the full price of pollution and, as a result, raises the total cost to the public of achieving the same cuts.

The bill sets statewide average emission rates rather than plant-by-plant limits, so heavily polluting plants could keep operating if cleaner plants offset them — and the second-phase limits could be cancelled entirely by Congress after a 1994 study, leaving the deepest cuts contingent on future legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits — less acid rain, cleaner diesel, cleaner tailpipes, and explicit ratepayer and low-income protections — are large and the bill took the concentrated interests' profits head-on. The honest cost case is real: ratepayers still pay through fees and uncovered rate increases, and the bill's rate-based, subsidy-heavy design would likely have delivered the cuts more expensively than the market-based sulfur-allowance trading system Congress ultimately adopted in 1990. The congressional escape hatch on phase two also made the long-term commitment softer than its headline numbers suggest.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee through a year of subcommittee hearings and was never reported for a floor vote, and its acid rain goal was instead enacted the next year inside the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 (H.R. 3030).

narrative.text: Representative Gerry Sikorski introduced the bill on March 16, 1989, with an unusually broad list of original cosponsors spanning both parties, and 158 members — 118 Democrats and 40 Republicans — eventually signed on.

The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, whose Health and the Environment subcommittee held hearings in April 1989, and the Energy and Power and Health and the Environment subcommittees held six more rounds of hearings between September and October 1989.
The full committee never reported the bill, and no committee or floor vote on it ever occurred.

The final action, on May 23, 1990, reads 'For Further Action See H.R. 3030' — the omnibus clean air bill that became the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, which wrote an acid rain program into law using sulfur-allowance trading rather than this bill's rate caps and subsidies.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning utilities and high-sulfur coal interests came out ahead in the near term: the committee stall bought them at least another year without mandated cuts. But the delay was not decisive, because an acid rain program became law anyway through H.R. 3030, and under that law utilities gained flexibility (tradable allowances) that this bill would have denied them — so the industry arguably ended up better off for having waited.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-burning utilities that gained time and flexibility

for.name: Gerry Sikorski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Acid Deposition Control Act of 1989 and recruited a large bipartisan original cosponsor list.

for.name: 40 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including moderate Republicans such as Sherwood Boehlert and Jim Leach.

for.name: President George H.W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Sent Congress an acid rain control proposal in 1989 and pressed for a comprehensive clean air bill, keeping pressure on committees to move legislation.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill out of subcommittee or reported it to the floor despite 158 cosponsors and repeated hearings; the record shows referrals and hearings only.

against.name: Coal-burning electric utilities
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against mandatory sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide cuts and the ratepayer-shifting fee-and-subsidy scheme.

against.name: High-sulfur coal producers
against.what_they_did: Opposed acid rain legislation that would cut demand for their coal.

against.name: Automakers
against.what_they_did: Resisted the bill's tighter tailpipe nitrogen oxide and hydrocarbon standards and onboard vapor-recovery requirements.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 158 cosponsors, including 118 of 257 House Democrats and 40 of 175 House Republicans — and the bill never reached a vote where party lines could have formed.

industries.note: The bill caps sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emission rates statewide and imposes fees on dirty generation, with federal subsidies only softening the residential rate impact. Utilities bore compliance costs they could not fully pass through, which is why they fought acid rain legislation.

Forcing power plants to cut sulfur dioxide emissions reduces demand for high-sulfur coal. The bill partly cushioned this by funding innovative control technologies chosen partly to prevent fuel switching, keeping coal in the mix.
The bill sets stricter tailpipe standards for nitrogen oxide and hydrocarbons and requires onboard vapor-recovery equipment on post-1991 vehicles — compliance costs the industry had long resisted.
A 0.05 percent sulfur cap on highway diesel after January 1, 1991 forces refiners to invest in desulfurization; the cleaner fuel directly cuts particulate and acid-rain pollution from trucks.
Generation from hydro and nuclear plants is exempt from the bill's fee, giving those sources a cost advantage over fossil generation as a side effect of the design.
